ai-9073325ad7.headline: Chip stocks slide after Broadcom boss likens AI investing to ‘casino’
ai-9073325ad7.fulltext:
Shares in semiconductor companies fell on Tuesday after the boss of Broadcom compared many AI investors to “casino” gamblers, and the Chinese memory chip maker CXMT said it had made good progress on a new chip architecture.
South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index tumbled 6.25% as investors dumped chip stocks, while other Asian markets were also lower. Japan’s Nikkei fell 1.8% and the Taiwan exchange lost almost 2%, with the country’s chip maker TSMC down by a similar amount.
Samsung Electronics shares dropped 7.4% on the South Korean exchange, while the memory chip maker SK Hynix was down 10%.
In Japan, the chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron fell 7.15%, while SoftBank Group, an OpenAI investor, lost 8.5%.
On Wall Street the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell more than 100 points, or 0.35%, to 30,556 after the open. Micron Technology slid 4.8%, Advanced Micro Devices dropped 1.4%, while Nvidia lost 0.8% and Broadcom slipped 0.2%.
However, the Dow Jones industrial average, which tracks 30 large US companies, rose nearly 0.4% in early trading, while the FTSE 100 index in London hit a three-week high on the back of gains in financial stocks, retreating oil prices and easing bond yields.
The UK’s leading share index rose 0.73% to 10,762. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, dropped 1.2% to $105.36 a barrel.
AI shares have been on a rollercoaster in recent months amid concerns that companies are spending eye-watering amounts on AI infrastructure, funded by debt.
The latest sell-off came after CXMT said it had made good progress on new Dram architecture that would boost memory density, with plans for a product rollout. Investors are worried that the company could challenge Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron, the world’s biggest memory chip makers.
CXMT, which had an impressive debut on the Shanghai stock market in late July, makes Dram chips, which store the data that other AI chips draw on for their calculations.
“The rout in chip stocks seems set to continue thanks once again to news from China,” said Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG.
“CXMT’s new developments remind investors of the huge competition in the sector.
“While great for customers who can enjoy the white heat of technological improvement and get falling margins into the bargain, it is dangerous for high-flying tech stocks who have promised so much, and on whom the entire stock market rally seems to rest.”
Hock Tan, the chief executive of the US chip maker Broadcom, said the AI boom had attracted investors who did not really understand what they were betting on.
“A lot of investors have no clue what they are investing in,” he said at a conference in Singapore, in comments reported by Bloomberg. They “set very extreme expectations only to find out that it’s almost like they are in a casino”.
AI companies such as the ChatGPT maker OpenAI are still lossmaking. Tan said OpenAI’s annualised revenues of $50bn (£38bn) at the end of September suggested a viable business model but offered little guarantee on long-term profitability.
“For now it’s still losing money because they’re spending a lot on training,” Tan said. “So frankly, it doesn’t tell anything at this point except that there is a lot of potential revenue growth out of providing frontier generative AI models.”
He noted that a sizeable portion of AI labs’ enterprise revenue came from pilot projects. “When you are a kid you go to a video arcade, you play,” he said. “Your parents give you $10 of tokens, you finish it in 10 minutes and you haven’t learned anything.”

indian-startups-677f0bab95.headline: Fundamentum Frontier Advisors Marks First Close Of ₹3,000 Cr Deeptech-Focused Fund
indian-startups-677f0bab95.fulltext: Ex-Fundamentum’s cofounder Ashish Kumar’s VC firm Fundamentum Frontier Advisors (F2A) has marked the first close of its growth-stage AI and deeptech fund at ₹3,000 Cr, India’s largest fund in the sector. Additionally, F2A said its LPs have approved plans to increase the size of the fund to ₹3,500 Cr, given the investor demand beyond the current capacity. The fund has raised capital from both domestic and overseas investors and will divide the funds across two vehicles. It plans to deploy the corpus into 12-15 companies over the next 2-3 years, writing cheques in the range of ₹100-200 Cr each. It claims to be in the advanced stages of closing three investments within the upcoming quarter. “More Indian companies are now building deeptech products for global markets, with India as their engineering and commercial base. Having worked with such companies from their early years, I have seen how much the right capital matters once the technology is validated and customers start to scale. We believe that is the stage at which F2A can help them become category leaders,” said general partner Debraj Banerjee. F2A was founded by Fundamentum Partnership partner and cofounder Ashish Kumar earlier this year. Kumar, Banerjee and Vivek Singla are F2A’s general partners while Fundamentum’s former general partner Nandan Nilekani is the anchor investor for the fund. The VC investor’s strategy focuses on three sectors: consumer business leveraging AI and frontier technologies, enterprise software, deeptech infrastructure and engineered systems. It targets India-domiciled companies earning revenue from India as well as globally. Despite the common involvement of team members including Kumar and Nilekani between Fundamentum and F2A, the two are separate legal entities. Notably, Fundamentum has itself launched its new fund this year – its third fund with a target corpus of ₹2,200 Cr. Deeptech is the latest investor darling as funding for the sector nearly tripled to $290 Mn across 28 deals in the quarter ending September 2026, as against $105 Mn across 29 deals a year ago, per Inc42’s ‘Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, Q3 2026’ report. The likes of South Korean gaming giant KRAFTON, global VC investor Accel, and Mumbai-based early-stage VC AUM Ventures have all mentioned plans to bet on this space in the past few months.

other-interests-62d9ae95f5.headline: OpenAI’s blockbuster Navier-Stokes proof isn’t what we thought it was
other-interests-62d9ae95f5.fulltext:
Mathematicians are finally making sense of the biggest event in decades for their field—and it’s stranger than anyone thought.
In early September OpenAI posted an inscrutable 166-page solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, one of math’s famed “million-dollar problems.” Initial accounts—including from the company itself—suggested that the proof, produced by an internal large language model (LLM), followed an approach devised by two Spanish mathematicians, Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa.

The model’s purported reliance on this “Spanish program” sparked a very public conflict between the company and Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at New York University. Buckmaster had spent much of the past year using LLMs to carry out that program alongside Levent Alpöge, an employee of OpenAI’s archrival, Anthropic. The pair cried foul after OpenAI—whose public models Buckmaster and Alpöge had been using—announced a Navier-Stokes proof that seemed to build upon and then leapfrog over their hard-won progress. But the resemblance between the two groups’ methods now seems merely skin-deep.
“When you go to the details, it is a different approach,” says Gonzalo Cao-Labora, a mathematician at EPFL, the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne. Scientific American spoke with several groups of experts working through the OpenAI paper. All said that it’s increasingly clear that the company’s proof does not follow the Spanish program.
The Navier-Stokes equations are the math behind every fluid. OpenAI solved the million-dollar problem by uncovering a flaw in the equations. The company’s artificial intelligence concocted a situation in which the equations declared that the speed of a fluid’s flow should be infinite—a so-called blowup that can’t happen in real life.
OpenAI solved the problem with an “agent swarm,” some 10,000 copies of its new, math-adept LLM, which spent about 88 hours of computing time and 130 billion tokens collectively constructing a blowup. The company’s math team threw all its resources at the problem after learning of significant progress made by Buckmaster and Alpöge. Buckmaster has alleged that OpenAI then attempted to bribe and threaten him to prevent him going public with insinuations of malfeasance, which he ultimately did.
Even top experts have found OpenAI’s proof of blowup to be completely impenetrable. But the agents coded their arguments into Lean, a programming language used to automatically verify that the logical steps toward a conclusion in a given sequence are all valid. Several prominent research groups are now using both the Lean code and the paper, with the help of other LLMs, to get a simplified, bird’s-eye view of the math involved.
The proof does somewhat resemble the Spanish program in that both exploit the same “loophole” in the official framing of the Navier-Stokes problem that was given by the Clay Mathematics Institute. It permits a mathematician to coax the equations into blowing up by constructing a weird, unphysical force that “stirs” the fluid just right. But closer examination reveals that OpenAI’s proof builds its unnatural force in a totally distinct way. The proof’s similarities to Buckmaster and Alpöge’s progress are superficial.
Of course, the OpenAI result’s novelty doesn’t mean it wasn’t influenced by the Spanish program. In fact, OpenAI initially used a smaller team of agents to prove an intermediate result, and some experts say that this more modest squad did follow the program. But the 10,000-agent swarm apparently realized a different path was required to finish the job. Of course, regardless of OpenAI’s insistence that its model couldn’t have seen Buckmaster’s data (which the company reiterated in a statement to Scientific American), the “black box” nature of LLMs means we’ll likely never know the swarm’s exact chain of reasoning.
“I honestly don’t see a factual resolution of this,” says Camillo De Lellis, a mathematician at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, N.J. “It’s not anymore a matter of clearly verifiable mathematical facts.”
What’s important, and perhaps a harbinger of math’s future, is how long it took experts to realize all this. When OpenAI revealed its landmark achievement on September 8, company officials clearly and repeatedly stated that their proof followed the Spanish program. Their combative exchange with Buckmaster before the release seems to suggest that they believed as much. And they weren’t initially certain whether his work had been incorporated in their model’s training data.
That is, OpenAI didn’t understand its own model’s proof. And still, more than a month later, no one fully does.
Last week the company dumped some 400 more results on the community. In the pre-AI era, at least a dozen of those results could have merited any human mathematician a Fields Medal—math’s Nobel Prize. There already aren’t enough experts on Earth to keep pace with the onslaught, and there’s no sign that it’s slowing down.

global-economics-f9eb89f74e.headline: Google launches flagship AI model Gemini 4 Argon for developers, businesses
global-economics-f9eb89f74e.fulltext:
[Text below is Insider's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
Google says it's back on the AI frontier, and now everyone can put that claim to the test.
The company announced on Tuesday that its new Gemini 4 model, dubbed "Argon," is rolling out to the public and will be available to Gemini app users and developers.
Google is positioning Argon as its new workhorse model, stating that it excels at coding, cybersecurity, and knowledge work in finance and law.
Tulsee Doshi, Gemini product lead at Google DeepMind, called Argon a "powerhouse" model and said it would be the first of a family of new Gemini models rolling out over time.
As is often the case with the most advanced AI models, Argon is available only to paying users. It's rolling out to Pro and Ultra Gemini app subscribers, meaning users will have to pay at least $19.99 per month to access it. Those subscribers will also see Argon in AI Mode while searching on Google. Developers will also need to pay for the new model.
Google first unveiled Argon last month, but it was only available to a set of trusted partners to proactively test it and address cyber vulnerabilities.
The new model arrives amid heated competition between the big AI companies. Meta said on Monday that its new Muse Wonder class of models would bring the company to the frontier, the industry term for the most advanced AI, while also powering its buzzy personal agent, Muse. Last month, OpenAI started rolling out its latest family of frontier models, GPT-6.
Argon gives Google an opportunity to reassert itself in the AI race after the company chose not to launch its previously-promised frontier model, Gemini 3.5 Pro.
Cornhole-playing robot
Google has been testing its new Gemini 4 model internally with employees for several weeks and said it had helped engineers increase the production of AI-generated code by 35%, while helping improve other Google products such as Chrome.
"I actually think it's been one of the biggest game changers for us," Doshi told Business Insider, referring to the increased amount of internal testing for Gemini 4. "Getting that feedback from Googlers who are using the model every day, I think has been both helpful in terms of just better understanding the model and better understanding its strengths and weaknesses."
Doshi said Argon was helping to speed up robotics development inside Google, thanks to the model's improved multimodal and reasoning skills. Google said it trained a robot to play cornhole by having Argon watch a human player and calculate joint movements and spatial coordinates.
Google also said it has stepped up efforts to prevent the model from behaving in ways it shouldn't, employing a system that tracks the model's chain of thought to determine if it's behaving. "I think that's actually really important because then you can actually intervene. You can say, 'Okay, the model is actually veering off in a way that's concerning. Let's stop here,'" said Doshi.
"I think that gives us a much more robust set of protections in launching this model."
While Google employees are already testing better versions of Argon internally, Doshi said the model rolling out will be the one the company announced benchmarks for last month. However, Google is making clear that this is just the start of its next big push.
"People should expect to see continued improvements coming from us wholesale," Doshi said.

agritech-fac1c6a9dc.headline: India’s food inflation surges to 7.74%, weak monsoon spikes prices amid El Niño risks | India News
agritech-fac1c6a9dc.fulltext:
India’s food inflation surges to 7.74%, weak monsoon spikes prices amid El Niño risks
Onion prices more than doubled over the year, with inflation accelerating to 108.09% in September from 48.78% in August
India’s food inflation surged to 7.74% in September from 5.97% in August, driven by a sharp spike in onion prices, rising ginger and garlic costs, and mounting risks to agricultural production from deficient rainfall. Economists warn the pressure could persist into 2027 if El Niño conditions intensify.
El Niño is a periodic warming of sea surface temperatures in the Eastern Pacific every two to seven years. It can last up to 12 months and affect rainfall and temperature patterns. The World Meteorological Organisation has warned this year’s El Niño may be stronger than anything since monitoring began and literally off the charts.
Onion prices more than doubled over the year, with inflation accelerating to 108.09% in September from 48.78% in August, according to National Statistics Office data released on Monday. Ginger inflation stood at 62.85%, garlic at 54.62% and lemon at 36.41%.
Deep Dive
The increase comes as India faces the prospect of a particularly strong El Niño that can weaken the monsoon. The country received its lowest June-September rainfall in more than a decade. The season’s rainfall was fourth-lowest since 2001 and 13th-lowest since 1901, as per India Meteorological Department data.
Parts of key agricultural states, including Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Punjab and Haryana, are facing extreme drought conditions, adding to concerns about crop output, soil moisture and reservoir levels.
“We reckon that beyond oil-related input costs, adverse weather is adding to food-price pressures, with El Niño potentially persisting into 2027,” said Emkay Global Financial Services lead economist Madhavi Arora.
Crop level issues
Crop-specific supply constraints are adding to the pressure on vegetables and spices. Garlic production in Rajasthan, one of the major producing states, is estimated at only about 60% of the previous year’s level, said Deepak Pareek, founder of HnyB, a consulting organisation. The production shortfall is tightening supplies and keeping prices elevated, he said.
Ginger prices are facing pressure from a combination of domestic supply losses and a firm international market. Pareek said last year’s crop was of poor quality, leading to losses during storage. Higher export prices, following a crop failure in Nigeria, are also increasing prices, while the health of the upcoming kharif crop is a concern, particularly in Maharashtra and Karnataka.
The Department of Consumer Affairs’ price-monitoring data point to pressure on household staples. On September 24, the average retail price of rice was ₹46.43 per kg, against ₹43.15 a year earlier. Tur dal cost ₹125.18 per kg, compared with ₹116.12, while packed groundnut oil was ₹210.04 per kg, against ₹188.53.
These increases suggest that pressure extends beyond a handful of vegetables, although prices are not rising uniformly across the food basket. Potato inflation remained negative at 11.50% in September. Tomato prices were 8.62% lower than a year earlier.
Global prices and a low base
The increase in food inflation also reflects movements in global commodity prices and the statistical base against which annual inflation is calculated.
Dipti Deshpande, senior director and principal economist at Crisil, said food prices had been the principal driver of inflation and that the increase was broadening beyond the food basket. She added food inflation reflected a low statistical base, surging onion prices and a near-synchronised rise in global prices of rice, wheat, maize, edible oils and sugar.
A low base can magnify the annual inflation rate when prices are compared with an unusually low level in the previous year. It does not, by itself, mean that prices have risen sharply in the latest month.
Global commodity prices also matter for India because imports influence domestic availability and costs, particularly for edible oils. Higher crude oil prices can add to the cost of transporting and producing food, including through fuel, fertilisers and other agricultural inputs.
Rabi crop at risk
The next test for food prices will be whether the rainfall deficit affects yields and the transition to the rabi season, when farmers sow crops harvested in spring. “Food inflation is likely to remain firm in the coming months as weak rainfall weighs on agricultural output,” Deshpande said.
She warned that bajra, tur, maize, groundnut, rice and soybean remain vulnerable in regions where rainfall deficits coincide with limited irrigation.
Concerns are also mounting over the rabi crop because of low soil-moisture levels and elevated temperatures.

india-c72f54c76b.headline: Shock, anger and a crackdown: why a contentious electoral revision has sparked outrage
india-c72f54c76b.fulltext:
Months of simmering public anger have given rise to a season of discontent in India. In its latest iteration, the demand is for the removal of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the scrapping of a controversial electoral rolls revision that has struck 130 million people off the register. Protests have erupted every day over the past week, prompting a violent crackdown on dissenters in the capital.
Over the weekend, Delhi was effectively under lockdown, transformed into a militarised landscape of barricades, road closures and paramilitary forces marching through the streets. Ahead of a protest led by the Cockroach Janta party on Saturday, authorities deployed a massive dragnet: 245 trains to Delhi were cancelled, 45 metro stations were shut, liquor shops were closed, internet services were cut off in the heart of the city and activists were put under house arrest.
The founders of the Cockroach party were removed from an Air India flight shortly after it landed at Delhi airport on Saturday. Opposition leaders were held for more than eight hours in various police stations. Video footage showed students and activists being manhandled, beaten and dragged off the streets while some journalists were also swept up in the detentions. A supreme court lawyer assisting those detained was carried away by police, his shirt torn in the process. The crackdown extended to Mumbai, where Tushar Gandhi, the great-grandson of Mahatma Gandhi, was whisked away by the police to prevent him from participating in a local demonstration. On Monday, the Delhi police denotified Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site, instead recommending three alternative locations.
“I have been in public life and have watched politics for four decades now, and I have never witnessed this kind of preparation for a demonstration. It was extraordinary by any stretch of the imagination,” political activist Yogendra Yadav, who was also detained, said of Saturday’s crackdown. Despite what he described as “terror unleashed by the state”, he said, small groups staged flash protests in several areas of Delhi defying the heavy security presence.
The crackdown was preceded by similarly aggressive police action against Congress party’s protests, led by Rahul Gandhi. Dramatic images of police personnel detaining Gandhi and his sister, Priyanka, amid scenes of chaos flashed across screens nationwide.
The ruling Bharatiya Janata party has defended its position, with spokesperson Ravi Shankar Prasad accusing the opposition of weaponising protests after electoral defeats. “One, Indian democracy has thwarted attempts to incite anarchy. Two, the country will be governed by parliament, not by the streets,” he said at a news briefing.
While suppression of protests is not new, what stands out this time is the scale of the crackdown in the capital. Government clampdowns in Indian-administered Kashmir have been far more severe, particularly in 2019, when sweeping restrictions were imposed after the revocation of Article 370.
The ferocity of the state response reflects the high political stakes for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government, which faces mounting resistance over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and questions about the credibility of the electoral process.
The latest protests began with a demand for Kumar’s resignation after an Indian Express investigation reported that the ECI’s two other commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had raised concerns about changes to electoral rolls, registration procedures, and digital systems. While Kumar has not responded to the investigation, the ECI said in a statement that “differing views” were part of the “decision-making process”. But the anger runs deeper. The SIR exercise has faced criticism for putting citizens through a trial by fire and leaving the most marginalised in a Kafkaesque limbo. Critics and opposition leaders have gone further, charging that the exercise was designed to benefit the ruling regime.
Former election commissioner Ashok Lavasa told me that the SIR process is unprecedented and unfair, marking a departure from the Commission’s traditional emphasis on inclusion. “For more than seven decades the ECI took it upon itself, as a duty, to enrol everyone who was eligible to vote. And that was one of the basic differences between how Indian democracy works and how other democracies function, where you need to apply to get enrolled,” he said. Voters accustomed to a “friendly procedure” now face a hostile system, which he said “is not good for democracy” in the long run.
Yadav argued that the SIR controversy has exposed what he describes as a deeper process of democratic capture by the ruling party. “Elections are the only mechanism now left for the regime to stamp its legitimacy and election capture is critical to their survival. And therefore, Gyanesh Kumar is critical,” he said. He pointed to a 2023 law giving election commissioners legal immunity for actions performed in their official capacity, which he said is broader than even the protection afforded to judges.
As to what comes next, he envisions potential for three strands to find common ground: the opposition parties, organised civil society groups, and ordinary citizens. For a government that has shown no sign of budging yet, he said, the calculus will get harder. “The longer they delay, the higher the stakes.”
On Monday, the Keralam assembly passed a resolution seeking Kumar’s removal, as opposition parties marched toward the supreme court demanding action against him. And the Cockroach movement and leftist student groups have vowed to continue protesting. “People have refused to be fearful any longer. They will come again and again,” said left-wing student leader, Danish Ali. “We are living in a democratic country, and protest is a fundamental right that no one can snatch away from us.”
What else we’re reading about
Human rights | South African jurist and former international criminal court judge, Navi Pillay, who is of Indian Tamil heritage, has won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. In a first-person account published in 2023, she wrote about her grandparents, who came from India and worked on a sugarcane farm in South Africa for five years before being allowed to buy land.
Technology | The United States has suspended labour-certification processing for several major technology companies, including top Indian IT firms, as part of a crackdown on what it alleges is a misuse of its flagship green card program, fraud and the displacement of American workers. The impacted companies include Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe. “We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies,” the US labour secretary Keith Sonderling announced last week.
Climate| Citing a significant rainfall deficit linked to the El Niño weather phenomenon, the Maharashtra government last week announced water cuts of at least 10% across urban areas starting 16 October. The state government had previously declared drought conditions in 74% of the sub-districts.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
With Delhi in the news for all the wrong reasons, I turned to Mayank Austen Soofi, who writes a daily Delhi column for Hindustan Times, to share a spot he returns to for a moment of reprieve. “Whenever I can, I spend a solitary afternoon at the tiny Sufi shrine of Hazrat Sarmad Shaheed, beside the Jama Masjid mosque. The bazaar outside the shrine is the Walled City’s noisiest quarter, yet inside one can sit in silence beneath the neem tree growing beside Sarmad’s grave. An Armenian Jew from Iran, Sarmad fell in love with a Hindu boy in Sindh, eventually became a naked fakir and settled in Mughal Delhi. Executed by Emperor Aurangzeb, his grave lies beneath a red cloth that recalls his blood-soaked beheading. These days, I linger a little longer at the resting place of a man who would just not submit to power.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
32
At least 32 children from the Indigenous community in Balaghat, Madhya Pradesh, have died since June, the Indian Express reported. An inquiry found evidence of measles and malaria. The children, aged between one and 13, experienced symptoms including high fever, skin rashes and abdominal pain.
Vibe check
For Mumbai-based cinematographer, Arbab Kamal Khan, the fleeting, unguarded moments of everyday life offer the most honest form of documentation. His Instagram account is an extension of this cinematic vision, capturing the languor of slow days, the beauty of the mundane and the quiet air of romance.
“When someone passes away, we don’t remember the curated moments,” he told me. “We always go back to the little things, the moments that are small or intricate.”
For me, the images and videos featuring his parents – their feet across each other besides teacups resting atop an Urdu newspaper, or his dad resting under his wife’s dupatta as she brushes her hair – are particularly striking because older people are rarely afforded such tenderness in visual culture. In his frames, his parents are not only elderly figures but also lovers who continue to find intimacy in each other’s presence.

ai-9e58dc3016.headline: Threat of AI share crash puts world financial stability at risk, says IMF
ai-9e58dc3016.fulltext:
The threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets is putting world financial stability at risk, the International Monetary fund has warned.
In its twice-yearly Global Financial Stability Report, the IMF highlighted the sky-high valuations for AI companies along with their increasing debt pile as one reason that risks in the system are “elevated”.
“The consequences of an AI correction could be global,” it warned. Aside from the US, Asian markets would be most exposed, and the UK and euro area potentially more insulated – though investors with US holdings would be hit.
Athanasios Vamvakidis, the deputy director of the IMF’s monetary and capital department, launching the report, said: “The exposure of the rest of the world to US assets, particularly AI, is the highest it has ever been. So this is supporting the global economy through wealth effects today; but if we get a market correction it could have broad implications.”
An AI crash was one of three “salient risks” to stability identified by the IMF, alongside rising government borrowing costs and the threat of a big cyber-attack.
It called this trio of factors “plausible near-term catalysts for a sharp tightening of financial conditions and market turmoil”.
The IMF’s analysis underlined the interconnected nature of big AI companies, and the high levels of borrowing being undertaken to fund investment in the sector.
“Weaker or less durable investment and profitability in AI could trigger a correction in AI-related asset prices, exacerbated by rising leverage, concentrated exposures, and circular financing arrangements,” it said.
Such a reassessment would then “sharply reduce investment, trigger equity market corrections, and tighten financial conditions, with global spillovers”.
The “magnificent seven” big tech stocks – Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla – account for more than 35% of the S&P 500 share index in the US, up from 12% a decade ago, and their total market capitalisation has increased by more than 50% in the past two years.
Yet the IMF warned of “growing evidence” that the successful rollout of AI “may not require investment on the massive scale being undertaken by ‘hyperscaler’ firms”, and “potential economic gains may not be as large as expected”.
The hyperscalers are the companies building the underlying infrastructure for the AI rollout, including many vast datacentres. They include Amazon Web Services, Google, Meta and Oracle.
Shares in semiconductor companies fell on Tuesday after the boss of Broadcom compared many AI investors to “casino” gamblers. Reports that the Chinese memory chip maker CXMT was making good progress on a new chip architecture also hit South Korean tech companies.
The IMF also highlighted the growing leverage, or borrowing, that underpins the current boom and could amplify the effects of a crash.
In particular, it identified soaring debts contracted by the companies themselves; hedge fund investment in the sector; and retail investors borrowing to speculate in AI stocks.
In the event of an AI-led market downturn “these growing sources of leverage heighten the potential for forced selling and surges in equity volatility”, it said.
It also pointed to the prevalence of “circular financing” deals, tying stronger AI companies to weaker partners in the same sector, and potentially exacerbating the impact of a share price correction.
It identified $300bn (£227bn) worth of transactions between hyperscalers and “weaker AI firms” in just the past three years, supplemented by $650bn in debt, in exchange for $1.4tn in future financial commitments.
In London, the chief executive of the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority, Nikhil Rathi, urged every small business across the financial sector to take out insurance to protect themselves against AI-related cybersecurity threats.
He told MPs on the Commons Treasury committee that not all companies would have the resources to pay for access to “frontier” AI models such as Anthropic’s Mythos, which has been released on a restricted basis after it was said to be rapidly identifying gaps in government and corporate cybersecurity systems.
“One message I’d give to every small business: you should consider making sure you are insured,” Rathi said.

ai-7c431d9eeb.headline: AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models
ai-7c431d9eeb.fulltext:
AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models
Most startups fail. A new industry is giving their data an afterlife in AI.
When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup this year, he didn’t think its data was worth much: the users were anonymous, the company just a few years old. But he’s since turned the firm’s digital archives into real money. He’s netted roughly $25,000 for his code base and a still-pending amount (likely around $15,000) for the workspace data in Google, Notion, Figma, and Slack. “At least all that stuff we were doing for two and a half years is worth something to someone somewhere,” he says.
The sale was brokered by a company called SimpleClosure, part of a new growth sector in tech: businesses catering to dying startups. Estimates from Carta and AngelList show shutdowns rising between 26% and 56% annually in recent years, and an end-of-life ecosystem—including coaches, “death doulas,” and firms that help handle the legal, tax, and operational headaches of going belly-up—has emerged. Now tech undertakers are selling the data remains to AI labs.
SimpleClosure added data sales to its services in April. Its Asset Hub platform helps founders sell their code and workspace data—emails, chats, documents. Buyers include foundation AI labs, vendors that construct simulated workspaces for AI training, and mature tech companies building their own models. Asset Hub has handled over 150 deals and expects to return over $10 million to startups by the end of 2026. CEO Dori Yona has seen these transactions, once rare and “somewhat taboo,” become increasingly routine, with 47% of SimpleClosure deals now including code or data sales.
And it’s got company. Industry rival Sunset also has a rapidly growing data resale business. Founder and CEO Brendan Mahony says Sunset values a dying client’s assets by head count, years in operation, volume of data, and how the team used its tools. Particle board, he says, is a good analogy: “This operational exhaust data is like the wood shavings that everyone thought had no value, but it actually has a ton.”
Demand for defunct companies’ data emerged suddenly last year, as AI training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets. Surge AI, for example, buys data to build “reinforcement-learning gyms” where clients’ AI agents practice tasks—think debugging a complex IT architecture or drafting appellate briefs. Nick Heiner, who leads the company’s work on these environments, says he seeks data archives reflecting a range of situations, from disagreements to tricky judgment calls. Heiner explains that one company’s Slack history, if it captures conversations with variety and depth, can be worth more than another’s Slack, email, and calendars combined.
Real archives avoid common errors in synthetic worlds, such as references to dates that don’t exist, but the extent of performance gains remains unclear. No company has yet released tests comparing results of real-world data training with the alternatives. Pricing reflects this uncertainty: Buyers quote wildly different numbers, Heiner says, because valuations are based on “research theses” estimating how many useful tasks come from, say, 100,000 lines of code.
That hasn’t stopped bigger deals from happening. This past August, as part of Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy, Google outbid the AI data company Mercor to buy the carrier’s decades of data, including 100 million emails, 500 million Teams messages, and 176,000 employee records. The price tag: $10 million. And Bloomberg reported in September that SpaceX’s AI unit is weighing buying data from struggling startups.
Legally, this all could get iffy. Spirit’s flight attendants’ union objected to the sale on privacy grounds, and Greg Ewing, an attorney who advises AI startups, has called such data “legally radioactive.” Suppliers employ data scientists to scrub personally identifiable information and exclude HR records, and buyers say they scrub too. But Ewing points out some of the private details that lurk in emails and calendars: doctor appointments, school pickup arrangements, date-night plans. He describes a “Wild West of AI training” that is only starting to give way to proper licensing agreements and vetted use.
There’s also the question of who profits from these windfalls. The proceeds typically flow to senior creditors and investors—not employees. To Ifeoma Ajunwa, a law professor at Emory University and author of The Quantified Worker, this represents a form of “captured capital.” Legal precedent allows for monitoring to help workers do their jobs, but once a firm is out of business, that justification vanishes. “Employers should have express consent before selling workers’ data,” says Ajunwa, but she adds that there’s no federal law banning such sales.
While many see this new market as a chance for failing businesses to recover some value, these wind-down sales also have limitations. Founders have little to no visibility into who is buying the data and what they plan to do with it. Plus, there’s little assurance they’re getting a fair offer. Data prices will likely stabilize in the coming year, though, unless an AI bubble pops first. Either way, tech’s new undertakers will be there to appraise what’s left.
Matthew King is a technology and environmental journalist based in Baltimore.

ai-ac3b4c5178.fulltext:
A robotic hand developed by Chinese startup LinkerBot is displayed at the World Robot Conference in Beijing in August.
Advanced humanoid hardware is one of the strategic high-tech fields where China has an early lead over the US.
The human hand is a marvel of evolutionary biomechanics. With an opposable thumb and four long dexterous fingers held together by 27 bones and 27 joints, it can grasp, clench and twist with extraordinary dexterity and delicacy. Despite decades of innovation, robotic replicas are still no match. Even today’s most cutting-edge metallic fingers fumble at shoelaces and keys.
That lack of precision is one of the main reasons the parade of jaw-dropping robotic feats in recent years – from choreographed kung fu moves to record-breaking 100-meter sprints – has yet to translate into meaningful commercial deployment. Alex Zhou, founder of a pioneering startup called LinkerBot, estimates that 20,000 humanoid robots were installed globally last year, but the number of actual working machines is in the low thousands. The rest are mainly for entertainment.
That won’t change, he says, until humanoids can replicate the capabilities of life-like hands. “Robot hands are the link between the machine and the physical world,” says Zhou, sporting spiky hair and a powder-blue summer jacket during an interview at LinkerBot’s headquarters in Beijing.

Amansa Investments, SBI Mutual Fund and HDFC Life Insurance Company, among others, have invested over Rs 413 crore in defence electronics maker Tonbo Imaging India Ltd through secondary share transactions, valuing the company at around Rs 4,000 crore.
This comes ahead of the company's Rs 852 crore Initial Public Offering (IPO).
The transactions, executed on September 29-30, involved existing investors CEAQ Singapore and CEAQ India transferring shares to a group of domestic and international institutional investors, according to the Red Herring Prospectus (RHP).
The buyers included Amansa Investments, Malabar India Fund, SBI Emergent India Fund, SBI Optimal Equity Fund, HDFC Life Insurance Company, Susquehanna Asia Technology, Valuequest Founders Conviction and 360 ONE Multi-Stage Defence and Space Fund, it showed.
Amansa Investments was the largest buyer, acquiring 24.32 lakh shares at Rs 700 apiece, the upper end of the IPO price band, for around Rs 170.24 crore.
Susquehanna Asia Technology Pty Ltd, Valuequest Founders Conviction LVF and 360 ONE Multi-Stage Defence and Space Fund each purchased 5.73 lakh shares for Rs 40.10 crore.
Akash Manek Bhanshali bought 5.66 lakh shares for Rs 39.59 crore, while SBI Emergent India Fund acquired 5 lakh shares worth Rs 35 crore. SBI Optimal Equity Fund and HDFC Life Insurance Company purchased shares valued Rs 20.09 crore and Rs 16.03 crore, respectively.
The company's IPO will open for public subscription on October 15 and close on October 19, with the price band of Rs 665-700 per share.
The issue comprises an Offer For Sale (OFS) of 1.22 crore equity shares by promoters and existing investors, with no fresh issue component.
Since the IPO is entirely an OFS, Tonbo Imaging will not receive any proceeds from the issue.
Founded in 2003 by technologists who had earlier worked with the US Department of Defense and Sarnoff Corporation, the company shifted its focus to defence product manufacturing in 2012 following a buyout by its current promoters.
Tonbo Imaging designs and manufactures sensing, processing, communication and guidance systems for surveillance, reconnaissance, targeting and control applications. Its product portfolio includes thermal imaging cores, weapon sights, handheld thermal imaging binoculars, targeting systems, missile seekers, fire control systems and missile guidance systems.

Huawei Technologies has shipped more than 100 million devices powered by its Kirin processors since 2023, when it returned to the smartphone market with a new generation of premium handsets. The company says testing of its next-generation Kirin 2027 chip is also progressing in line with expectations.
The company disclosed the figure on Tuesday as it unveiled new details about its flagship Kirin 9050 series, the first mass-produced chip using its proprietary LogicFolding architecture, developed under a framework it calls the Tau Scaling Law.
Chinese media outlet Yicai reported on Tuesday that Huawei had also begun testing its next-generation Kirin 2027 processor, with preliminary results meeting the company’s targets. The report cited Xu Songyu, a director responsible for wireless device chips at Huawei’s semiconductor business.
Speaking at a press briefing on Tuesday in Shanghai, Xu said progress on LogicFolding had surpassed Huawei’s expectations despite early uncertainty over whether the technology could be manufactured at scale while maintaining production yields, according to Yicai.
The company did not immediately respond to the South China Morning Post’s request for comment.
LogicFolding is a technique under Huawei’s Tau Scaling Law, which was announced in May. The approach proposes a major shift in semiconductor development by improving how quickly data moves between parts of a chip and across a computing system.
The strategy aims to extract more computing power through optimised semiconductor designs without relying on the most advanced chipmaking equipment, particularly the world’s cutting-edge lithography tools blocked by US-led export controls.
Huawei is also expanding its business in semiconductors used to power artificial intelligence systems, with its Ascend AI chips gaining ground in the Chinese market as Washington’s restrictions limit access to the most advanced American processors.
The company shipped 572,000 AI accelerators in the first half of 2026, ‌up from more than 300,000 a year earlier, capturing a 28 per cent share of China’s data centre AI chip market, according to research firm IDC data reported by Reuters. AI accelerators are specialised processors used to train and run AI models.
Nvidia shipped 678,000 AI accelerators in China over the same period, giving it 34 per cent of the market, down from 44 per cent a year ago, Reuters reported, citing IDC, which declined to comment on the data.
Huawei’s chip ambitions suffered a setback in 2020 when tighter US sanctions barred the company from using the foundry services of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. The company returned with its home-grown Kirin 9000s processor in 2023, which powered its Mate 60 Pro smartphone.

India Considers Local Manufacturing Mandate For Solar Inverters, Batteries
New Delhi, Oct 13 (KNN) The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy is examining proposals to mandate domestically manufactured solar inverters and introduce minimum local content requirements for batteries under the next phase of the PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana.
The proposed changes aim to expand domestic manufacturing, reduce import dependence and create business opportunities for Indian solar equipment and battery manufacturers. The requirements are still under consideration and have not been finalised.
Local Content Rules May Be Expanded
Existing domestic content requirements primarily cover solar modules and cells in government-supported projects. The proposed changes could extend localisation requirements to inverters, batteries and related components used in rooftop solar installations.
The ministry is reviewing industry suggestions before deciding the final requirements. The current phase of the scheme runs until March 2027.
Scheme Targets One Crore Households
Launched in February 2024, the PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana has an approved outlay of Rs 75,021 crore and aims to install rooftop solar systems in one crore households.
The scheme seeks to help households generate solar electricity and reduce their dependence on grid power. Subsidies are linked to installed capacity, with assistance of Rs 30,000 for a 1 kW system, Rs 60,000 for a 2 kW system and Rs 78,000 for systems of 3 kW or above.
The programme targets approximately 30 GW of residential rooftop solar capacity.
Push To Strengthen Domestic Supply Chains
India remains dependent on imports for several lithium-ion battery materials, including lithium, cathodes and anodes. The proposed localisation requirements could encourage domestic production of battery packs, energy storage components and solar power electronics.
The government has also introduced production-linked incentive schemes to support domestic solar manufacturing and advanced battery production.
However, localisation could initially increase procurement costs if domestic manufacturing capacity is insufficient to meet demand.
Implications For Manufacturers
The proposed rules could affect companies operating across solar equipment, battery manufacturing and energy storage. Waaree Energies and Premier Energies operate in solar manufacturing, while Exide Industries and Amara Raja Energy & Mobility have businesses in batteries and energy storage.
The impact would depend on the final domestic content thresholds, implementation timelines and eligibility criteria. Manufacturers may also need additional investment in production capacity, technology and supply chains to meet the proposed requirements.

The 0.4% fee on Unified Payments Interface transactions above Rs 2,000 to merchants will be imposed after the Hindu festival of Diwali, which will be celebrated on November 8 this year, said the National Payments Corporation of India on Tuesday.
The corporation is an umbrella body of retail payments and settlement systems operating under the Reserve Bank of India.
On September 14 and September 15, the Ministry of Finance issued notifications stating that UPI payments to merchants valued above Rs 2,000 would attract a merchant discount rate of 0.4%.
A merchant discount rate is a fee charged to businesses by banks to cover the costs of processing transactions. The rate typically ranges from 1% to 3% of the transaction value for credit card payments and can be up to 0.9% for debit card transactions.
On September 28, the Union government said that the charges would take effect on October 15.
The National Payments Corporation of India said on Tuesday that the decision to defer the implementation of the charges was taken “keeping in mind the festive season”.
Opposition to the charges
In September, a petition had been filed before the Supreme Court that said that businesses may pass on the additional cost of the UPI charges to consumers.
Additional Solicitor General N Venkataraman, appearing for the Union government, had submitted before the court on September 28 that 96% of transactions would not attract the charge.
In 2025-’26, transactions exceeding Rs 2,000 accounted for just 4% of person-to-merchant UPI payment, The Indian Express reported. However, these transactions represented nearly two-thirds of the total value of person-to-merchant UPI payments.
On September 15, the government clarified that the 0.4% fee had been capped at Rs 300 per transaction for payments of Rs 75,000 and more. The Ministry of Finance had said that the new framework will have no impact on person-to-person transactions, “irrespective of the amount transferred”.
It had also “advised” banks to ensure that the charges are not passed on to the customers.
The government’s notification on UPI transactions had sparked concerns among the Opposition parties, retailers and consumers.
The Opposition has demanded that the Union government roll back the charges on UPI payments.
On September 23, several traders and shopkeepers in Madhya Pradesh also staged a protest against the government move by covering the quick response code or QR code and requesting customers to pay in cash.

The Technology Development Board (TDB) under the Ministry of Science and Technology has agreed to provide INR 86 crore in financial support to Bengaluru-based Peptris Technologies Pvt. Ltd. to advance four AI-discovered drug candidates through preclinical development and toward clinical trials.
The project, titled VIGOR — Moving AI-Discovered Molecules from the Lab to the Clinic, has a total cost of INR 172 crore. The funding will be provided through the Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund as optionally convertible debt (OCD), according to an official statement.
The program aims to advance the four experimental drug candidates from Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 4 to TRL 6, involving experimental validation, preclinical studies and preparation for clinical development.

The VIGOR program covers four experimental drug candidates targeting different therapeutic areas:
PEPR111: Neuromuscular disorders and cancer
PEPRX101: Hair loss (alopecia)
PEPR202: Neuropathy
PEPR112: Diabetes mellitus
All four candidates are currently at TRL 4, with the project targeting progression to TRL 6. The development process will combine Peptris’ proprietary AI-powered drug discovery platform with laboratory validation and established drug development processes.
The company also plans to use a global contract research organization (CRO) network to support the development and validation of the candidates.
TDB Funding to Support Preclinical Development
Rajesh Kumar Pathak, Secretary of TDB, said artificial intelligence has the potential to change how pharmaceutical researchers identify and develop new drugs. He added that TDB is supporting technology-intensive programs through the RDI Fund to bridge the gap between innovation and clinical development and strengthen India’s capabilities in biotechnology, pharmaceuticals and AI-based healthcare innovation.
A Peptris representative said the financial support would help the company advance its VIGOR program through critical preclinical development stages, combining AI-driven discovery with experimental validation.
Bridging AI Discovery and Drug Development
AI-based drug discovery enables researchers to identify promising molecules and investigate disease mechanisms. However, candidates identified computationally must undergo experimental testing and preclinical evaluation before they can progress toward human clinical trials.
The VIGOR program focuses on moving selected AI-discovered molecules through these development stages. The proposed work is intended to establish the scientific and preclinical evidence needed to determine whether the candidates can advance further in the drug development pipeline.

other-interests-21f5992cef.fulltext:
For the past two years, scientists studying the health of forests, grasslands and swamps have been worried. Since 2023, the amount of carbon dioxide Earth’s landscapes have been able to absorb has dropped dramatically in the face of extreme weather, resulting in a record jump in atmospheric CO2 concentrations in two successive years.
But 2025 has bucked that worrying trend, with preliminary research revealing a strong rebound in the land carbon sink and a corresponding decline in the growth rate of atmospheric CO2.
Terrestrial ecosystems such as forests and grasslands take up CO2 from the atmosphere as they grow, and emit carbon when they decompose or burn. Over recent decades, these ecosystems have tended to absorb more CO2 than they have released, due to warmer temperatures and the fertilising effect of CO2, which boosts plant growth. This creates a global carbon sink that varies in strength from year to year.
Advertisement
“In 2023 and 2024, because of El Niño and the Amazon fires, we had the almost cancellation of the global land sink,” says Philippe Ciais at the Climate and Environment Sciences Laboratory in France, who led the analysis. “This cancellation led to a very high CO2 growth rate, because if CO2 is not taken by land, it stays in the atmosphere.”
Ciais and his colleagues estimate that the land sink absorbed 2.36 gigatonnes of carbon in 2025. This is 0.71 gigatonnes more than the 2015-2022 average.
This recovery was driven largely by a dramatic return of growth in tropical forests. “The climate became more normal, especially in Africa and the Amazon, so the plants recovered their carbon uptake capacity,” says Ciais.
Researchers estimate that natural sinks in the oceans and on land have removed over half of the CO2 emitted by human activities. But this benefit won’t last forever, and scientists expect the world’s land biosphere to shift from being a carbon sink to a carbon source within the next several decades unless human-driven emissions taper off.
The sudden disappearance of the land sink in 2023 and 2024 had researchers worried that the sink was collapsing decades earlier than expected.
2024 was an “extreme year”, says team member Mike O’Sullivan at the University of Exeter in the UK. The “massive recovery” in 2025 is therefore good news, he says. But he warns we don’t know if this recovery effort can be sustained indefinitely, especially if weather patterns become increasingly extreme.
The super El Niño already under way in the Pacific is expected to become the most intense in history later this year, bringing extreme heat and drought to crucial terrestrial sinks such as the Amazon rainforest. This means another sharp slump in carbon uptake is expected next year.
Such a cycle of repeated weather shocks, fuelled by climate change, may be weakening the global land sink’s long-term ability to store carbon, warns O’Sullivan. This sink is already 25 per cent smaller than it would have been without the effects of climate change and natural variability, researchers estimate.
“The land is showing short-term resilience,” says O’Sullivan. “There is a short-term shock, which is the El Niño, and it is recovering the year after. There is strong evidence of that happening. What it doesn’t mean is that the land is going to maintain long-term resilience to climate change.”

ai-b70ca8133d.fulltext:
Gemini 4 Argon is now available worldwide as Google's most capable frontier model
Google is rolling out Gemini 4 Argon globally, making its new flagship AI model available to developers, businesses, and consumers starting today.
Gemini 4 Argon is accessible through the API in AI Studio and the Gemini platform, according to Google. Google AI Ultra subscribers can use the model in Google Antigravity, while AI Ultra and Pro subscribers get access through the Gemini app and Google Search's AI mode.
Not everyone benefits equally, though. Free Gemini users and paying Plus subscribers now only have access to the weaker Flash models under a new model tier structure. Argon replaces the Gemini Pro class as Google's new frontier series. Google says more Gemini 4 models will follow, which likely means updated Flash variants that would eventually trickle down to free and Plus users as well. Internally, Google is reportedly already testing a potential successor codenamed "Carbon," which is supposed to outperform Argon at coding in particular.
Pricing and benchmark results remain as previously reported: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens at the introductory rate, with a 95 percent discount on cached inputs. Argon holds the top spot on the Vals Index, but it still trails Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 in independent overall rankings. And because Google waited roughly two weeks to ship, it now also sits behind Meta's Muse Wonder Full, which launched just yesterday.
*Google doesn't state this figure explicitly but says the cache is 95 percent cheaper than the regular input token price.
Google says Argon turned months of internal engineering into weeks
Google shared some internal numbers with the launch, though they're self-reported. Software engineers using Argon increased agent-driven code submissions by more than 35 percent, while code rollbacks dropped by nearly a third, the company says.
In the Chromium project, Argon helped the Chrome team complete an architectural refactor across hundreds of files within the 40-million-line codebase. Work that would have taken months was finished in a few weeks. For users, the payoff is that web pages can move between tabs, sidebars, and floating windows without needing to reload.
Working with Google's open-source Agent Development Kit, Argon ran autonomously overnight and found optimizations that cut session preparation time by 40 percent and sped up cold imports by 21 percent. Inference speed for the open Gemma models on an A100 via vLLM jumped by a factor of 2.85, from roughly 37,900 to over 108,000 tokens per second. The changes are visible in upstream pull requests.
Argon can also generate complex 3D models, games, and animations in pure code that run directly in the browser. One demo features a raytracing engine written entirely in Python with no external libraries. Google published the source code.
In the demo below, Argon starts from a single image in Antigravity and controls Blender via MCP in an autonomous loop. It modeled gothic architecture and set up audio-reactive lighting to produce a finished 3D scene, Google says.
3D remains a weak spot for Meta's Muse models, which according to Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang were not specifically trained for 3D demo games.
Google offers 10,000 researchers free access and claims its strongest safety record yet
Google is also offering 10,000 researchers the highest usage tier of Google Antigravity free for six months. Spots are awarded on a rolling basis depending on eligibility, capacity, and selection. Applications are open now.
Cybersecurity defenders can apply separately for the Fairwind program, which grants access to Argon without cyber safeguards. Google plans to expand the program to hundreds of additional partners.
On the safety side, Google calls Argon's architecture its strongest to date. External red teaming in the bio domain bypassed fewer than 1 percent of tested safety checks, and on an adversarial set, violations dropped by nearly half compared to earlier Gemini models.
On agent alignment, attempts to take unauthorized shortcuts fell to 2 percent. An automated misalignment monitor analyzes the agent's reasoning and actions in real time.
Argon also scored the lowest attack rate on the Gray Swan Indirect Prompt Injection benchmark, with a successful attack rate of just 0.7 percent across 15 adaptive attempts. In the previous Gray Swan test, GPT-6 Astra hit 8.5 percent and Claude Opus 5 came in at 4.8 percent. Google's write-up doesn't make clear whether the exact same tests were used, though. More safety details are available in the model card.

world-c72f54c76b.headline: Shock, anger and a crackdown: why a contentious electoral revision has sparked outrage
world-c72f54c76b.fulltext:
Months of simmering public anger have given rise to a season of discontent in India. In its latest iteration, the demand is for the removal of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the scrapping of a controversial electoral rolls revision that has struck 130 million people off the register. Protests have erupted every day over the past week, prompting a violent crackdown on dissenters in the capital.
Over the weekend, Delhi was effectively under lockdown, transformed into a militarised landscape of barricades, road closures and paramilitary forces marching through the streets. Ahead of a protest led by the Cockroach Janta party on Saturday, authorities deployed a massive dragnet: 245 trains to Delhi were cancelled, 45 metro stations were shut, liquor shops were closed, internet services were cut off in the heart of the city and activists were put under house arrest.
The founders of the Cockroach party were removed from an Air India flight shortly after it landed at Delhi airport on Saturday. Opposition leaders were held for more than eight hours in various police stations. Video footage showed students and activists being manhandled, beaten and dragged off the streets while some journalists were also swept up in the detentions. A supreme court lawyer assisting those detained was carried away by police, his shirt torn in the process. The crackdown extended to Mumbai, where Tushar Gandhi, the great-grandson of Mahatma Gandhi, was whisked away by the police to prevent him from participating in a local demonstration. On Monday, the Delhi police denotified Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site, instead recommending three alternative locations.
“I have been in public life and have watched politics for four decades now, and I have never witnessed this kind of preparation for a demonstration. It was extraordinary by any stretch of the imagination,” political activist Yogendra Yadav, who was also detained, said of Saturday’s crackdown. Despite what he described as “terror unleashed by the state”, he said, small groups staged flash protests in several areas of Delhi defying the heavy security presence.
The crackdown was preceded by similarly aggressive police action against Congress party’s protests, led by Rahul Gandhi. Dramatic images of police personnel detaining Gandhi and his sister, Priyanka, amid scenes of chaos flashed across screens nationwide.
The ruling Bharatiya Janata party has defended its position, with spokesperson Ravi Shankar Prasad accusing the opposition of weaponising protests after electoral defeats. “One, Indian democracy has thwarted attempts to incite anarchy. Two, the country will be governed by parliament, not by the streets,” he said at a news briefing.
While suppression of protests is not new, what stands out this time is the scale of the crackdown in the capital. Government clampdowns in Indian-administered Kashmir have been far more severe, particularly in 2019, when sweeping restrictions were imposed after the revocation of Article 370.
The ferocity of the state response reflects the high political stakes for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government, which faces mounting resistance over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and questions about the credibility of the electoral process.
The latest protests began with a demand for Kumar’s resignation after an Indian Express investigation reported that the ECI’s two other commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had raised concerns about changes to electoral rolls, registration procedures, and digital systems. While Kumar has not responded to the investigation, the ECI said in a statement that “differing views” were part of the “decision-making process”. But the anger runs deeper. The SIR exercise has faced criticism for putting citizens through a trial by fire and leaving the most marginalised in a Kafkaesque limbo. Critics and opposition leaders have gone further, charging that the exercise was designed to benefit the ruling regime.
Former election commissioner Ashok Lavasa told me that the SIR process is unprecedented and unfair, marking a departure from the Commission’s traditional emphasis on inclusion. “For more than seven decades the ECI took it upon itself, as a duty, to enrol everyone who was eligible to vote. And that was one of the basic differences between how Indian democracy works and how other democracies function, where you need to apply to get enrolled,” he said. Voters accustomed to a “friendly procedure” now face a hostile system, which he said “is not good for democracy” in the long run.
Yadav argued that the SIR controversy has exposed what he describes as a deeper process of democratic capture by the ruling party. “Elections are the only mechanism now left for the regime to stamp its legitimacy and election capture is critical to their survival. And therefore, Gyanesh Kumar is critical,” he said. He pointed to a 2023 law giving election commissioners legal immunity for actions performed in their official capacity, which he said is broader than even the protection afforded to judges.
As to what comes next, he envisions potential for three strands to find common ground: the opposition parties, organised civil society groups, and ordinary citizens. For a government that has shown no sign of budging yet, he said, the calculus will get harder. “The longer they delay, the higher the stakes.”
On Monday, the Keralam assembly passed a resolution seeking Kumar’s removal, as opposition parties marched toward the supreme court demanding action against him. And the Cockroach movement and leftist student groups have vowed to continue protesting. “People have refused to be fearful any longer. They will come again and again,” said left-wing student leader, Danish Ali. “We are living in a democratic country, and protest is a fundamental right that no one can snatch away from us.”
What else we’re reading about
Human rights | South African jurist and former international criminal court judge, Navi Pillay, who is of Indian Tamil heritage, has won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. In a first-person account published in 2023, she wrote about her grandparents, who came from India and worked on a sugarcane farm in South Africa for five years before being allowed to buy land.
Technology | The United States has suspended labour-certification processing for several major technology companies, including top Indian IT firms, as part of a crackdown on what it alleges is a misuse of its flagship green card program, fraud and the displacement of American workers. The impacted companies include Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe. “We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies,” the US labour secretary Keith Sonderling announced last week.
Climate| Citing a significant rainfall deficit linked to the El Niño weather phenomenon, the Maharashtra government last week announced water cuts of at least 10% across urban areas starting 16 October. The state government had previously declared drought conditions in 74% of the sub-districts.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
With Delhi in the news for all the wrong reasons, I turned to Mayank Austen Soofi, who writes a daily Delhi column for Hindustan Times, to share a spot he returns to for a moment of reprieve. “Whenever I can, I spend a solitary afternoon at the tiny Sufi shrine of Hazrat Sarmad Shaheed, beside the Jama Masjid mosque. The bazaar outside the shrine is the Walled City’s noisiest quarter, yet inside one can sit in silence beneath the neem tree growing beside Sarmad’s grave. An Armenian Jew from Iran, Sarmad fell in love with a Hindu boy in Sindh, eventually became a naked fakir and settled in Mughal Delhi. Executed by Emperor Aurangzeb, his grave lies beneath a red cloth that recalls his blood-soaked beheading. These days, I linger a little longer at the resting place of a man who would just not submit to power.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
32
At least 32 children from the Indigenous community in Balaghat, Madhya Pradesh, have died since June, the Indian Express reported. An inquiry found evidence of measles and malaria. The children, aged between one and 13, experienced symptoms including high fever, skin rashes and abdominal pain.
Vibe check
For Mumbai-based cinematographer, Arbab Kamal Khan, the fleeting, unguarded moments of everyday life offer the most honest form of documentation. His Instagram account is an extension of this cinematic vision, capturing the languor of slow days, the beauty of the mundane and the quiet air of romance.
“When someone passes away, we don’t remember the curated moments,” he told me. “We always go back to the little things, the moments that are small or intricate.”
For me, the images and videos featuring his parents – their feet across each other besides teacups resting atop an Urdu newspaper, or his dad resting under his wife’s dupatta as she brushes her hair – are particularly striking because older people are rarely afforded such tenderness in visual culture. In his frames, his parents are not only elderly figures but also lovers who continue to find intimacy in each other’s presence.

“The consequences of an AI correction could be global,” it warned. Aside from the US, Asian markets would be most exposed, and the UK and euro area potentially more insulated – though investors with US holdings would be hit.
Athanasios Vamvakidis, the deputy director of the IMF’s monetary and capital department, launching the report, said: “The exposure of the rest of the world to US assets, particularly AI, is the highest it has ever been. So this is supporting the global economy through wealth effects today; but if we get a market correction it could have broad implications.”
An AI crash was one of three “salient risks” to stability identified by the IMF, alongside rising government borrowing costs and the threat of a big cyber-attack.
It called this trio of factors “plausible near-term catalysts for a sharp tightening of financial conditions and market turmoil”.
The IMF’s analysis underlined the interconnected nature of big AI companies, and the high levels of borrowing being undertaken to fund investment in the sector.
“Weaker or less durable investment and profitability in AI could trigger a correction in AI-related asset prices, exacerbated by rising leverage, concentrated exposures, and circular financing arrangements,” it said.
Such a reassessment would then “sharply reduce investment, trigger equity market corrections, and tighten financial conditions, with global spillovers”.
The “magnificent seven” big tech stocks – Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla – account for more than 35% of the S&P 500 share index in the US, up from 12% a decade ago, and their total market capitalisation has increased by more than 50% in the past two years.
Yet the IMF warned of “growing evidence” that the successful rollout of AI “may not require investment on the massive scale being undertaken by ‘hyperscaler’ firms”, and “potential economic gains may not be as large as expected”.
The hyperscalers are the companies building the underlying infrastructure for the AI rollout, including many vast datacentres. They include Amazon Web Services, Google, Meta and Oracle.
Shares in semiconductor companies fell on Tuesday after the boss of Broadcom compared many AI investors to “casino” gamblers. Reports that the Chinese memory chip maker CXMT was making good progress on a new chip architecture also hit South Korean tech companies.
The IMF also highlighted the growing leverage, or borrowing, that underpins the current boom and could amplify the effects of a crash.
In particular, it identified soaring debts contracted by the companies themselves; hedge fund investment in the sector; and retail investors borrowing to speculate in AI stocks.
In the event of an AI-led market downturn “these growing sources of leverage heighten the potential for forced selling and surges in equity volatility”, it said.
It also pointed to the prevalence of “circular financing” deals, tying stronger AI companies to weaker partners in the same sector, and potentially exacerbating the impact of a share price correction.
It identified $300bn (£227bn) worth of transactions between hyperscalers and “weaker AI firms” in just the past three years, supplemented by $650bn in debt, in exchange for $1.4tn in future financial commitments.
In London, the chief executive of the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority, Nikhil Rathi, urged every small business across the financial sector to take out insurance to protect themselves against AI-related cybersecurity threats.
He told MPs on the Commons Treasury committee that not all companies would have the resources to pay for access to “frontier” AI models such as Anthropic’s Mythos, which has been released on a restricted basis after it was said to be rapidly identifying gaps in government and corporate cybersecurity systems.
“One message I’d give to every small business: you should consider making sure you are insured,” Rathi said.

South Korean Hyundai Motor Group has committed to invest $15.5 billion in India between 2026 and 2032 through a dedicated investment entity, spanning manufacturing capacity expansion, research and development, local supplier development and investments in startups.
In a statement released on Tuesday evening, the group said the investment which will cover both Hyundai Motor India and Kia was discussed during a meeting between executive chair Euisun Chung and Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi. The investment is expected to create additional employment opportunities across manufacturing, R&D, engineering and supply chains, as per its statement.
The commitment, the group's largest investment pledge for India, comes two years after its automobile unit, Hyundai Motor India, raised ₹27,870 crore through its initial public offering in October 2024. During Hyundai India's first investor day last year in October, the company committed $5.4 billion investment till FY30.
The latest investment follows a ₹77,500 crore commitment for five years by Japanese auto giant Suzuki earlier in August, underlining the growing interest of global automakers in expanding their presence in India.
“India remains one of Hyundai Motor Group’s most important and strategic markets globally. The past 30 years have been defined by our commitment to India. This investment reaffirms our commitment to India for the next 30 years and beyond,” Chung said in the statement.
The investment commitments come after a strong year for India's passenger vehicle market, supported by the goods and services tax (GST) cuts announced last year. Passenger vehicle sales grew 8% year-on-year to about 4.6 million units in FY26, according to the Society of Indian Automobile Manufacturers (Siam).
The company said the investment will span manufacturing, research and development, supplier localization and new mobility businesses.
On the manufacturing front, it said the group plans to expand capacity at Hyundai Motor India and Kia India to cater to rising demand and strengthen India's role as an export base. The group currently has an annual production capacity of more than 1.4 million vehicles across Hyundai's Chennai and Pune facilities and Kia's Anantapur plant.
Alongside manufacturing, the group plans to invest about $700 million in its Indian R&D centre, including a vehicle testing track, to develop next generation automotive technologies. It said that the investment is aimed at strengthening local engineering capabilities and positioning India as a research and innovation hub for the group.
The group also plans to deepen its local supplier network through investments in regional partners, with a focus on increasing parts localization as it prepares for expansion of its electric vehicle portfolio.
“The group aims to lead India's future mobility ecosystem through strategic investments in emerging opportunities. This includes support for high-potential startups and expansion into new mobility services integrated with its core vehicle business,” the statement read.
The investment commitment comes as Hyundai Motor Group looks to strengthen its position in India, where its flagship carmaker has been losing ground to domestic rivals. Hyundai Motor India’s domestic sales fell 2% to 584,906 units in FY26, pushing it to fourth place in the industry rankings after 16 years as the country’s second-largest carmaker. The company has acknowledged that a slower pace of new model launches and upgrades than its rivals hurt its performance.
The group has also identified India as a strategic market for its next phase of growth. In January 2026, Hyundai Motor India appointed Tarun Garg as its first Indian managing director and chief executive officer, as the company prepared to step up investments in manufacturing, localization and new products.
Kia India, the group’s other passenger vehicle business in the country, has established itself among the top six carmakers since entering India in August 2019, nearly 23 years after Hyundai began operations in 1996.
The investment push also comes as both brands prepare to expand their product portfolios. Hyundai Motor India plans 26 product launches by 2030, including seven new nameplates, spanning different powertrains and vehicle segments.
Kia, meanwhile, plans to expand its Indian line up to 10 models by 2030, of which eight will be electrified vehicles, including electric and hybrid models. Its latest investor day strategy targets annual sales of 410,000 units in India by 2030.
