Centre postpones rollout of UPI payments fee above Rs 2,000 to after Diwali
While the charges were scheduled to take effect on October 15, the NPCI said its implementation was deferred ‘keeping in mind the festive season’.
The 0.4% fee on Unified Payments Interface transactions above Rs 2,000 to merchants will be imposed after the Hindu festival of Diwali, which will be celebrated on November 8 this year, said the National Payments Corporation of India on Tuesday.
The corporation is an umbrella body of retail payments and settlement systems operating under the Reserve Bank of India.
On September 14 and September 15, the Ministry of Finance issued notifications stating that UPI payments to merchants valued above Rs 2,000 would attract a merchant discount rate of 0.4%.
A merchant discount rate is a fee charged to businesses by banks to cover the costs of processing transactions. The rate typically ranges from 1% to 3% of the transaction value for credit card payments and can be up to 0.9% for debit card transactions.
On September 28, the Union government said that the charges would take effect on October 15.
The National Payments Corporation of India said on Tuesday that the decision to defer the implementation of the charges was taken “keeping in mind the festive season”.
Opposition to the charges
In September, a petition had been filed before the Supreme Court that said that businesses may pass on the additional cost of the UPI charges to consumers.
Additional Solicitor General N Venkataraman, appearing for the Union government, had submitted before the court on September 28 that 96% of transactions would not attract the charge.
In 2025-’26, transactions exceeding Rs 2,000 accounted for just 4% of person-to-merchant UPI payment, The Indian Express reported. However, these transactions represented nearly two-thirds of the total value of person-to-merchant UPI payments.
On September 15, the government clarified that the 0.4% fee had been capped at Rs 300 per transaction for payments of Rs 75,000 and more. The Ministry of Finance had said that the new framework will have no impact on person-to-person transactions, “irrespective of the amount transferred”.
It had also “advised” banks to ensure that the charges are not passed on to the customers.
The government’s notification on UPI transactions had sparked concerns among the Opposition parties, retailers and consumers.
The Opposition has demanded that the Union government roll back the charges on UPI payments.
On September 23, several traders and shopkeepers in Madhya Pradesh also staged a protest against the government move by covering the quick response code or QR code and requesting customers to pay in cash.
Written by Sneha. Edited by Tanya Shrivastava.

Pope Leo was diagnosed with a common form of lung cancer after doctors removed a lower lobe of his right lung in surgery on Tuesday, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin.
The 71-year-old pontiff has lung adenocarcinoma, with tissue tests conducted during the operation confirming what doctors had suspected from preparatory examinations, the bulletin said.
The pope was admitted to Rome’s Gemelli hospital on Tuesday for surgery ‌to remove a growth on his lung that doctors found in a recent health check-up.
The Vatican had said earlier on Tuesday evening that the surgery had been successful before providing a more detailed update from the pope’s lead surgeon, Professor Stefano Margaritora, the chief of thoracic surgery at the Gemelli.
“In order to make the procedure curative, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique,” Margaritora’s update said.
“A rapid intraoperative histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, as had been suspected from the preoperative tests,” it said.
Tuesday’s surgery lasted about 90 minutes and was ⁠successful with no complications, the Vatican said. The pope has woken up normally and is resting in his hospital room.
Leo left the Vatican ahead of the surgery shortly before 1pm in Rome and was seen waving from the back of a black SUV as his convoy drove about 9km (5.6 miles) north of the ‌Vatican to the Gemelli.
Upon arrival at the hospital, Leo shook hands with several officials, walked in front of a waiting crowd ⁠of well-wishers, some of whom shouted “Auguri” (best wishes), ⁠and headed in via the main entrance.
The Vatican said earlier this week that the pope was expected to recover in hospital for about a week. All his public events have been cancelled until October ‌20.
Leo, elected by the world’s cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to be a smoker or to have had recent health ‌issues.
The late ‌Pope Francis, Leo’s predecessor, was hospitalised several times as he grew frail in his later years. He died aged 88 in April 2025.
Leo, who spoke ‌in a firm, clear voice at his only public event on Monday, keeps a very busy schedule. He is due to make an 11-day tour of Uruguay, ⁠Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17.
The pope is the ultimate earthly authority for the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics and does not have a deputy ⁠who steps in when he is sick.
When a pope is incapacitated, the business of the Vatican’s vast bureaucracy carries on as usual, delaying any decisions that require papal approval.
Leo, born in Chicago in 1955 as Robert Prevost, served for decades as a missionary and ‌bishop in Peru before becoming pope. In 1985, ‌when he was a young priest, he came down with typhoid fever in Chulucanas, Peru and was hospitalised.
He recounted the experience in his only major interview given as pope, in a book for Penguin Peru.
Leo said the pain was so bad that he asked God to die rather than continue suffering. He took his survival as a sign from God that “We need you here [on Earth]”, he said.

Pope diagnosed with lung cancer but had successful surgery, Vatican says
- Published
Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer but had successful surgery to remove a lower lobe of his right lung, the Vatican has said in a medical bulletin.
The 71-year-old underwent a 90 minute surgery on Tuesday at Rome's Gemelli Hospital and was subsequently diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma.
"The operation was successful and there were no complications," the Vatican said. "After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it added.
The lump was first detected during what the Vatican has described as "routine checks". The Pope is expected to remain in hospital for about a week.
Earlier, large crowds waited for hours outside the hospital for the Pope.
They cheered greetings and well wishes as he passed, while he waved and smiled back through the lowered back window of his car.
He was then met by staff on the hospital steps. "I'm sorry," one of them commiserated, to which the Pope gave a smile and a shrug. "We're here for you," he was assured.
In its statement, the Vatican said the whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical".
A Vatican source told Agence France-Presse news agency further tests were being carried out to see if there was any sign the cancer had spread.
It was Leo XIV himself who on Sunday announced news of his operation to the world, speaking from the balcony in St Peter's Square after delivering the traditional Angelus blessing.
He said the nodule, or growth, on his lung was "contained" and had been found "at a very early stage", but that doctors had advised him to have it removed.
Gemelli's thoracic surgery team operated on the Pope, whose schedule has already been cleared until 20 October to give him time to recover.
Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was pulmonary adenocarcinoma, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said.
The Vatican has stressed that the pontiff, who is generally thought to be fit, had no symptoms of infection or illness.
Cardinal Kikuchi Tarcisio Isao of Tokyo wrote on social media that he'd had an audience with Pope Leo on Monday, and said the pontiff felt "nothing wrong" physically.
He said the Pope had decided to check in for surgery as soon as possible because he was due to travel to Latin America in early November, and was keen to stick to that plan.
The trip is particularly significant because it includes a visit to Peru, where the pontiff was a missionary and then a Bishop for many years.
Despite all the reassurances, the news has shaken Catholics all over the world.
"Am I worried? Yes, because I certainly wasn't expecting anything like this," Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Parolin told journalists on Tuesday.
He agreed that the news was like a "bolt from the blue", but said the cardinals had been struck by the Pope's "serenity" and were confident in his recovery.
Outside Gemelli Hospital, which has treated several popes and is home to a large statue of John Paul II, a few Catholics lingered after the pontiff was admitted.
Carla had come specially, wanting to be close.
"He seems calm, so we are calm too - even though illness is always unpleasant," she told the BBC. "We will wait here and pray."
"I was in St Peter's Square when he made the announcement, and I felt really awful," said Elsa, who was also present. "I was really taken aback," she said, explaining that when Pope Leo was elected she had thought he was a younger, healthier pontiff.
"It turns out he's vulnerable too," she added.

'Brutal session' for chip stocks shows AI trade is turning
In Asia, selling of Korean chipmaker shares extended into a fifth straight day on Tuesday, accelerating sharply, with the KOSPI index falling more than 6% while in Tokyo memory-maker Kioxia, down 13%, led AI-related losses.
Nearly four years since the launch of OpenAI's ChatGPT, cash has streamed into semiconductor companies, data centre owners, cable companies and anyone reaping revenues from an unprecedented race to build computing infrastructure.
Cracks in those bets, which began in June are now widening across markets, with a data centre IPO collapsing last week in Australia and credit investors becoming picky on AI debt.
In Asia, selling of Korean chipmaker shares extended into a fifth straight day on Tuesday, accelerating sharply, with the KOSPI index falling more than 6 per cent while in Tokyo memory-maker Kioxia, down 13 per cent, led AI-related losses.
"The most important development has been not just bond yields going up, but the volatility for bonds ... and that's starting to work its way out through asset pricing across the board," said Damien Boey, portfolio strategist at Wilson Asset Management in Sydney.
"It's a very uncomfortable situation on many fronts ... maybe AI capex just comes off the boil a little bit, and maybe a few players are casualties in that."
The US benchmark Philadelphia semiconductor index dropped 2.7 per cent on Monday and even heavier selling drove Seoul-listed chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix down by 10 per cent and 8 per cent , respectively.
On Monday, the research arm of BlackRock, the world's biggest asset manager, downgraded its US stocks outlook to neutral, citing "potential volatility around the AI buildout" and turned bullish on short-term Treasuries.
"The consequences of an AI correction could be global," the International Monetary Fund warned on Tuesday in its latest financial stability report.
The IMF called out AI's contribution to growth but said there was growing evidence that capability investments and economic gains may not be as big as expected.
Cost of capital
Caution is also coursing through primary markets.
Last week, Firmus, a data centre operator backed by Nvidia , shelved a $5 billion IPO in Australia as investor interest shrivelled, underscoring how suddenly risks are becoming the chief focus in allocating capital to the sector.
Tuesday's dollar and dim sum bond sale by Tencent Holdings in Hong Kong was the latest deal in debt markets' sights, with guidance for 10-year dollar notes about 1.15 percentage points on top of Treasury yields, which sit at 5.2 per cent .
Japan's tech investor SoftBank last month sold the biggest high-yield debt pile ever and promised to pay as much as 9.75 per cent on $4.5 billion it raised at a 7-1/2 year tenor.
The mood shift was front of mind at a slew of top financial conferences in Singapore, most recently on Monday when Broadcom's CEO said capital was the biggest constraint on growth.
To be sure, few are calling time on the AI trade altogether and on Monday Meta shares jumped 3.4 per cent on the release of a new AI model, but many see semiconductors as a warning sign.
Marc Velan, head of investments at Lucerne Asset Management in Singapore, believes the "brutal session" in Korea said more about positioning and the cost of capital than about any fundamental deterioration in AI demand.
"I suspect we're entering the next phase of the AI cycle, where markets increasingly focus on monetisation and returns on invested capital - I wouldn't call this the end of the AI trade," Velan said. "But Korea could be an early warning of a broader shakeout."
